title: Video Games: How They Are Made
summary: How teams of designers, artists, programmers, sound makers, and testers build a video game step by step, from a simple test version to a finished game.
poll: Making a video game is harder than playing one.

versions.title: How a Game Is Made
versions.text:
Do you like to play games on a screen? Lots of kids do. But how is a game made?

Some games are made by one person. Big games need a team. The team may have lots of people. It can take years!

Each person has a job. Some think up the rules. They plan what you do in the game. An artist draws the hero and the world. Some write the code. Code tells the game what to do.

Some make the sounds. They make the songs, the steps, and the jumps.

First, the team makes a small test game. It is plain. It may just use blocks. Kids play it. They say what is fun and what is not. Then the team fixes it.

Next, the team builds the real game. Then they test it a lot. They look for a bug. A bug is a mistake. It can make the game stop! They fix each bug they find.

At last, the game is done. Kids can play it. But the team still fixes bugs and adds new parts.

Lots of kids in Saudi Arabia now learn to make games, too!

versions.title: Video Games: How They Are Made
versions.text:
Millions of people around the world play video games every day. A game may look simple on the screen, but making it can be a huge job.

Some small games are made by just one person. Big games, however, need large teams. A team may have hundreds of people, and it can take several years to finish one game.

Each team member has a special job. Game designers plan the rules, the goals, and the levels. Artists draw the characters and build the worlds, often as 3D models. Programmers write the code, which is a set of instructions that tells the computer what to do. Sound designers and composers create the music and sound effects.

Most teams use a game engine. An engine is a set of software tools that already knows how to show pictures, play sounds, and make objects fall or bounce. This saves the team from starting from zero.

The first step is to build a prototype, a simple test version of the game. It might use plain gray blocks instead of finished art. Then players try it and give feedback about what is fun and what is confusing. The team uses the feedback to make changes.

Next, the team builds the full game. Testers play it again and again to find bugs, which are mistakes in the code. A bug might let a hero walk through a wall! Programmers fix each bug.

Even after the game is released, the team keeps fixing bugs and adding new levels.

In Saudi Arabia, more and more young people are now learning to design and program games.

Millions of people around the world play video games every day, and although a game may appear simple on the screen, creating it can be an enormous and complicated project.

Some small games are produced by a single person, but major games require large teams that may include hundreds of people, and completing one game can take several years. To succeed, these specialists must collaborate closely.

Each team member has a specialized role. Game designers plan the rules, objectives, and levels, while artists illustrate the characters and construct the environments, frequently as three-dimensional models. Programmers write the code, a set of instructions that tells the computer exactly how the game should respond whenever a player presses a button, which is what makes a game interactive. Sound designers and composers create the music and sound effects.

Most teams rely on a game engine, a collection of software tools that already knows how to render images, play sounds, and make objects fall or bounce realistically. An engine draws a fresh picture, called a frame, many times every second, often thirty or sixty times, so movement looks smooth.

Next, the team develops the complete game, and testers play it repeatedly to discover bugs, which are errors in the code. A bug might allow a character to walk through a solid wall! Programmers then correct each bug.

Even after the game is released, the team continues correcting bugs and adding new levels, characters, and challenges for players. In Saudi Arabia, an increasing number of young people are studying how to design and program their own games.

versions.text:
Millions of people around the world play video games every day, and although a game may appear simple on the screen, creating it can be an enormous and extraordinarily complicated undertaking.

Each team member has a specialized responsibility. Game designers determine the rules, objectives, and levels, while artists illustrate the characters and construct the environments, frequently as three-dimensional models. Development begins with a prototype, a simplified experimental version that might use plain gray blocks instead of finished artwork. A bug might allow a character to walk through a solid wall! versions.title: Video Games: How They Are Made
versions.text:
Millions upon millions of people across the globe play video games on a daily basis, and although a game may appear deceptively simple once displayed upon the screen, the process of actually creating it can constitute an enormous and remarkably intricate undertaking.

Certain modest games are produced entirely by a single determined individual, yet major commercial titles typically require sprawling teams that may encompass several hundred professionals, and bringing a single game to completion can readily consume several years of sustained effort. In order to succeed under such conditions, these diverse specialists must collaborate closely and communicate constantly throughout the entirety of the development process.

Each individual team member carries a specialized area of responsibility. Game designers determine the fundamental rules, overarching objectives, and individual levels, while artists illustrate the characters and construct the surrounding environments, frequently rendered as detailed three-dimensional models. Programmers write the underlying code, a comprehensive set of instructions that tells the computer precisely how the game ought to respond whenever a player presses any given button, which is ultimately what renders a game genuinely interactive rather than merely a passive animation. Sound designers and composers, meanwhile, produce the accompanying music and sound effects that render each virtual environment convincingly believable.

Most development teams rely heavily upon a game engine, a sophisticated collection of software tools that already understands how to render images, play sounds, and simulate physical objects falling or bouncing with realistic behavior, and it generates a fresh image, formally termed a frame, many times every single second, typically either thirty or sixty times, so that resulting motion appears smooth and visually continuous to the human eye.

Development characteristically begins with a prototype, a deliberately simplified experimental version that might substitute plain gray blocks in place of finished artwork. Players subsequently experiment with this prototype and provide candid feedback regarding which particular elements feel genuinely enjoyable, confusing, or frustrating, and the development team refines the underlying design through repeated iteration, systematically evaluating and modifying the game again and again until it meets their standards.

Subsequently, the team develops the complete, fully realized game, and dedicated quality-assurance testers play through it repeatedly in order to discover bugs, which are simply errors embedded within the underlying code. A single bug might, for instance, inadvertently allow a character to walk straight through an ostensibly solid wall. Programmers then painstakingly investigate and correct each individual bug, a meticulous process that can readily occupy several months before the finished game is finally released to the general public.

Even after a game's official release, the development team continues correcting residual bugs and adding substantial new content, such as additional characters and fresh challenges, over subsequent months or years. In Saudi Arabia, an increasing number of ambitious young people are now formally studying how to design and program their own interactive entertainment, and the capital, Riyadh, has hosted the Esports World Cup, one of the largest international video game competitions in existence, a development that vividly demonstrates the industry's rapidly growing economic and cultural significance throughout the Kingdom.

versions.title: Video Games: How They Are Made
versions.text:
Millions upon millions of people across the entire globe play video games on a strictly daily basis, and although any given game may appear deceptively simple once fully displayed upon the screen, the underlying process of actually creating it can constitute an enormous and remarkably intricate technical undertaking spanning numerous disciplines.

Certain modest, independently produced games are created entirely by a single determined individual working alone, yet major commercial titles typically require sprawling, specialized teams that may encompass several hundred professionals, and bringing a single ambitious game to completion can readily consume several years of sustained, coordinated effort. In order to succeed under such demanding conditions, these diverse specialists must collaborate closely across disciplinary boundaries and communicate constantly throughout the entirety of an often lengthy development process.

Each individual team member carries a clearly delineated area of specialized responsibility. Game designers determine the fundamental rules, overarching objectives, and individual levels of challenge, while artists illustrate the characters and meticulously construct the surrounding virtual environments, frequently rendered as intricately detailed three-dimensional digital models. Programmers write the underlying source code, a comprehensive set of precise instructions that tells the computer exactly how the game ought to respond whenever a player presses any given button, which is ultimately what renders a game genuinely interactive rather than merely a passive, predetermined animation sequence. Sound designers and composers, meanwhile, produce the accompanying musical score and sound effects that render each virtual environment convincingly immersive and believable to the player.

Most development teams rely heavily upon a preexisting game engine, a sophisticated and extensive collection of software tools that already understands, at a technical level, how to render images, play synchronized sounds, and simulate physical objects falling or bouncing with convincingly realistic behavior, and this engine generates a fresh image, formally termed a frame, many times over every single second, typically either thirty or sixty separate times, so that the resulting motion appears smooth and visually continuous to the human eye rather than jarringly disjointed.

Development characteristically commences with a prototype, a deliberately simplified experimental version that might substitute plain, unadorned gray blocks in place of finished, polished artwork. Players subsequently experiment extensively with this early prototype and provide candid, often blunt feedback regarding precisely which particular elements feel genuinely enjoyable, needlessly confusing, or outright frustrating, and the development team refines the underlying design through a process of repeated iteration, systematically evaluating and modifying the evolving game again and again until it satisfactorily meets their exacting internal standards.

Subsequently, the team develops the complete, fully realized game in its entirety, and dedicated quality-assurance testers play through it repeatedly and exhaustively in order to discover bugs, which are simply unintended errors embedded within the underlying source code. A single such bug might, for instance, inadvertently allow a player's character to walk straight through an ostensibly solid wall without any resistance whatsoever. Programmers must then painstakingly investigate and correct each individual bug in turn, a meticulous and often time-consuming process that can readily occupy several months before the finished game is finally released to the waiting general public.

Even well after a game's official commercial release, the development team invariably continues correcting any residual bugs and adding substantial new content, such as additional playable characters and fresh challenges, over subsequent months or even years of ongoing support. In Saudi Arabia, an increasing number of ambitious young people are now formally studying how to design and program their own original interactive entertainment, and the capital, Riyadh, has hosted the Esports World Cup, one of the largest international video game competitions currently in existence, a development that vividly and concretely demonstrates the industry's rapidly growing economic and cultural significance throughout the Kingdom.

HIGH.prompt: The article says specialists must collaborate closely. Explain why teamwork is so important in making a video game, using at least two examples from the article.
checklist: I used at least two examples of roles or stages.
I showed how the roles depend on each other.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Teamwork is essential in making a video game because each specialist depends on the others to finish the project. For example, programmers must collaborate with artists, since the code has to render the 3D models the artists create so that characters and worlds actually appear on screen. Likewise, sound designers depend on the game engine programmers build, because the engine is what plays the music and sound effects during each frame of the game. Without this collaborative relationship between roles, the interactive experience that players enjoy would never come together.
